headline: Highest risk is data leakage from broad network-egress pairings; prompt-injection and cascading-error risks are otherwise limited by the profiles.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Authelia exposes OIDC/ForwardAuth and EMQX exposes an HTTP API, but neither profile shows a shared filesystem, clipboard, or MCP bridge, so direct prompt injection is not evidenced. The only plausible bridge is manual or API-mediated content flow, which makes hijack possible but not default. Uncertainty remains because both are unverified docs-only profiles.
conditions: IF an operator copies EMQX-generated content into Authelia-managed policy text or prompts, injection becomes possible.
IF either agent is placed behind a shared message queue or filesystem bridge, attacker-controlled content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces and avoid copy-paste bridges.
Require human review of any text flowing from EMQX into Authelia.
Strip instructions from inbound payloads before forwarding them.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all cross-agent messages.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress, and EMQX touches IoT data while Authelia handles authentication flows via OIDC/ForwardAuth. No shared workspace is documented, but the pair can still leak sensitive context if operators route data through either service or if logs/requests are forwarded externally. Because the interaction is inferred from docs-only profiles, uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF IoT payloads or auth assertions are forwarded through either service, those contents can leave the local boundary.
IF logs from Authelia or EMQX are exported to a third-party backend, sensitive metadata may be exposed.
mitigations: Disable verbose request logging on both services.
Review outbound destinations for both agents.
Redact tokens, identifiers, and payload bodies before export.
Separate credentials and API keys per service.
requires-engineering: enforce egress allowlists.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Authelia and EMQX both have broad network egress, but neither profile shows filesystem write, git mutation, or overlapping mutable OAuth scopes. That makes direct capability conflict unlikely in the documented configuration. The main overlap is read/write to external APIs, which is not enough for a higher severity without additional write surfaces.
conditions: IF both agents are granted write access to the same external API or database, write conflicts can occur.
IF an orchestrator adds shared filesystem writes, concurrent mutation risk increases.
mitigations: Assign separate API credentials to each service.
Avoid shared mutable backends unless locking exists.
Schedule writes from only one agent at a time.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency controls.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Authelia can emit authentication decisions through OIDC/ForwardAuth, and EMQX can consume HTTP API inputs, so a downstream workflow could treat one agent's output as authoritative. No verification or human-in-the-loop step is documented, and both profiles are docs-only, so the safest reading is that a misclassification could cascade into incorrect actions or routing decisions.
conditions: IF EMQX consumes Authelia-derived identity or authorization decisions without verification, errors can cascade.
IF Authelia policy outputs are used to automate downstream routing, a bad decision can propagate.
mitigations: Add a manual approval step for high-impact decisions.
Cross-check identity or policy outputs against a second source.
Log and review rejected or anomalous decisions.
Limit automation to non-destructive actions.
requires-engineering: add schema validation and confidence thresholds.

E_compliance.rationale: Authelia is an authentication component and EMQX touches IoT data, but the profiles do not show PHI, EU-only residency, or a certification mismatch. The only documented compliance-relevant difference is data class exposure on EMQX, so the pair presents a modest policy-management risk rather than a clear residency or regulatory breach.
conditions: IF regulated IoT telemetry is routed through EMQX and retained alongside authentication logs, policy review is needed.
IF either service is deployed in a jurisdiction with stricter residency rules, storage locations must be checked.
mitigations: Classify the data handled by each service.
Review retention settings for logs and telemetry.
Confirm deployment region for both services.
Separate auth logs from IoT payload storage.
requires-engineering: implement data-residency controls.
